opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a great question, and it's something we think about a lot. GDPval was deliberately designed with highly specified tasks. We worked with experienced professionals across a range of occupations to write tasks that represent real work products, things like a legal brief, an engineering drawing, or a nursing care plan, and we gave the model everything it needed up front. That was the right starting point because it let us measure something concrete: given a well-defined assignment, how does the model's output compare to what an expert would produce?

But that's not how most real work happens. In practice, a huge part of a professional's job is figuring out what the task even is. You get an ambiguous request from your manager or a client, you have to ask clarifying questions, track down the right context, and iterate. Often the hardest part isn't producing the deliverable; it's knowing which deliverable is actually needed.

So I think benchmarks need to evolve in a few directions.

The first is **underspecification and interactivity**. We want to measure whether a model can take a vague request, recognize what's missing, and either ask good questions or make reasonable assumptions and flag them. That's a really different skill from executing a clean prompt.

The second is **longer horizons**. Many GDPval tasks take an expert a few hours. A lot of meaningful work spans days or weeks: managing a project, maintaining a codebase, following up with stakeholders. We need evaluations that capture whether a model can stay coherent and make progress over those timescales, including recovering from its own mistakes.

The third is **context and tools**. Real work happens inside an environment: your company's documents, email, internal systems, the history of decisions that were made. Benchmarks that give the model access to a realistic workspace, rather than a self-contained prompt, will tell us much more about actual usefulness.

And finally, **collaboration**. Most work is done with other people. So how well does a model work alongside a human, hand things off, take feedback, and fit into a team's workflow? That's hard to grade, but I think it's ultimately what matters most for economic impact.

The tricky part with all of this is that as tasks get more realistic, they get harder to grade reliably. Highly specified tasks are easier to judge consistently. So a big part of the research challenge is building grading methods, whether expert human review, model-based graders, or some combination, that stay trustworthy as the tasks get messier. But I think that's exactly where the field needs to go if we want benchmarks that keep tracking what these models can really do in the world.

r001.rationale: The response says benchmarks should test models handling vague requests from a manager or client, including identifying missing information and asking clarifying questions—matching the ambiguity a manager may leave to a human report.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is something I think about a lot. GDPval was deliberately built around well-specified tasks—a clear deliverable, a clear brief, a clear expert who could judge the output. We did that on purpose, because it let us measure something real and reproducible across forty-four occupations. But that design choice also means we're capturing a slice of work, not the whole thing. Most real jobs aren't handed to you as a tidy prompt with a reference deliverable attached.

So the first direction I'd want benchmarks to go is toward underspecified work. In practice, a huge part of being good at a job is figuring out what the task actually is—asking the right clarifying questions, noticing that the brief you were given is subtly wrong, pushing back when the request doesn't make sense. Right now most evals penalize a model for asking questions, because the grader just wants an answer. I think we need evaluations where the right move sometimes is to go back to the stakeholder, and where that gets rewarded rather than treated as a failure to complete.

The second thing is time horizon and continuity. GDPval tasks are roughly bounded—something a professional might do in a few hours to a few days. But real work compounds. You make a decision in week one that constrains what you can do in week six. You have to keep context across many sessions, remember what a client said three months ago, revise your own earlier output when new information arrives. Measuring that means building evaluations that unfold over long sequences of interactions, with memory and state, and where the quality of early decisions only becomes visible later. That's expensive and messy to build, but I think it's where the real signal is.

Third, I'd want to see more collaborative and multi-stakeholder settings. Almost no one does economically valuable work alone. You're coordinating with a team, you're negotiating with people who have different incentives, you're managing up and down. A model that produces a technically excellent deliverable but can't operate inside an organization isn't actually doing the job. So evaluations where the model has to work with other agents, or with simulated colleagues who are imperfect, inconsistent, or even adversarial—that gets closer to reality.

And then there's grading. One of the hardest parts of GDPval was getting expert graders to compare outputs reliably, and even there we found a lot of disagreement among experts. As tasks get more open-ended, "which is better" gets harder to answer. I think the field needs to invest much more in understanding what good judgment looks like in a domain—not just whether the output matches a reference, but whether the process was sound, whether the risks were flagged, whether the model knew the limits of its own knowledge. Some of that can be automated, but I suspect we'll always need a human-in-the-loop component for the frontier of what we're measuring.

The last thing I'd say is that we should be honest that the goalposts move. Any benchmark, once it's public, starts getting optimized against, and it stops telling you what it used to. So I don't think of GDPval as a finished thing. I think of it as a first draft of a measurement approach—one where the question "how much of this job can a model actually do, as judged by someone who does it" is the north star, and the specific tasks and formats are just the current best approximation we've got. The goal is to keep ratcheting toward tasks that look more and more like the real thing, even when that makes them harder to score cleanly.

r001.rationale: The response proposes evaluating models on underspecified work, including figuring out what the task is and asking clarifying questions—communicating the ambiguity a manager may leave to a human report.

astra-6.text:
I think the next step is to move from “Can you complete a well-specified task?” to “Can you figure out what the task should be, and then carry it through?” In real work, you rarely get all the context neatly packaged. You might get a vague request, have to ask a clarifying question, find the relevant information, and make decisions about what matters.

So I’d want benchmarks that capture that whole process, including collaboration. Can the model recognize when it needs input from a person? Can it incorporate feedback, handle changing requirements, and produce something that someone can actually use?

The challenge is keeping those evaluations rigorous. Once there are multiple reasonable paths to an outcome, checking against a single reference answer becomes less useful. You need to evaluate whether the result meets the underlying need, and how much human effort it took to get there. Highly specified tasks give us a useful starting point, but the broader question is whether these systems can help people accomplish work in the messy settings where that work actually happens.

r001.rationale: The response proposes evaluating whether models can handle vague requests, incomplete context, and determine what task needs doing, which conveys the ambiguity a manager might leave to a human report.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the next step is to move from “Can you complete this well-specified task?” to “Can you figure out what work needs to be done?” In real work, you rarely get a perfect prompt with all the relevant files attached and a clear definition of success. You get an ambiguous request, you have to find context, ask the right questions, and make judgment calls.

So I’d want benchmarks that capture more of that process: longer interactions, changing requirements, and collaboration with a person. Does the model recognize when it’s missing something? Does it ask a useful clarifying question? Can it incorporate feedback without losing track of the original objective?

And then we need to evaluate the outcome in context. A polished document isn’t necessarily useful if it solves the wrong problem. The question is whether the work actually helps someone accomplish what they intended, and how much supervision it took to get there.

r001.rationale: The response proposes moving beyond well-specified tasks to ambiguous real-work requests where the model must identify what needs doing, find context, and make judgment calls. This conveys the task ambiguity described by the criterion.
